title: The old repertoire
summary: Bring back every piece from season one in one week, one or two a sitting, and notice what stayed.
materials: the piece from your teacher, with a pencil

figure.alt: A row of twelve boxes, one for each of the twelve pieces learned across season one's twelve weeks, brought back one or two at a time this week to see which pieces come back fastest.

steps.title: The old repertoire
steps.body:
A piece you learned months ago and never touched again quietly fades. A piece you come back to once mostly stays, and comes back faster the second time than it took to learn the first time. This week tests every piece from the very first season at once.

1. List every piece you learned in season one, from memory if you can, checking old recordings if you need to.
2. Play one or two of them each sitting, hard bars first if a piece feels rusty.
3. By the last sitting, try playing all of them once through, one after another, if time allows.
4. Notice which pieces came back fastest, and think about why: were they shorter, more played since, or just better learned the first time?

Retrieval is not testing what you remember for its own sake. It is what keeps a piece from ever really being lost.

figure.alt: The same twelve boxes, one or two played each sitting, noticing which ones came back fastest and why.

steps.title: Four sittings
steps.body: Fifteen minutes each. Tick a sitting when it is done. Days do not matter; sittings do.
checklist: Sitting 1: list every season one piece, play the first two
Sitting 2: play two more, hard bars first for any that feel rusty
Sitting 3: play the remaining pieces, one or two at a time
Sitting 4: play as many as possible in a row, then one as if recording
The very first piece from season one, played once, just to hear it again

steps.title: Record this week's version
steps.prompt: Say the names, then play two season one pieces back to back, hands in the frame.

extras.title: A medley of old pieces
extras.body:
Join two old pieces together with a short bridge you write yourself.

Start with a question: what four bars would carry a listener from the end of one piece into the start of another?

Three constraints: four bars for the bridge, a key that fits both pieces, and a clean ending on the second piece's first note.

Sketch first: write out the bridge's notes before you try to play it.

You know it works when you can play both pieces and the bridge in one go, without stopping.
